'''Tommie Harris Jr.''' (born April 29, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] for eight seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[University of Oklahoma]], and was recognized as a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] twice. The [[Chicago Bears]] chose him in the first round of the [[2004 NFL draft]], and he also played a season for the [[San Diego Chargers]].  He was a three-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection.

'''Thomas Allen Thayer''' (born August 16, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (American football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[United States Football League]] (USFL). He played in the NFL for the [[Chicago Bears]] and the [[Miami Dolphins]], and won a [[Super Bowl]] as a member of the 1985 Chicago Bears. Prior to his NFL career, Thayer played in the USFL for the [[Chicago Blitz]], [[Arizona Wranglers]] and the [[Arizona Outlaws]] from 1983 to 1985. He is currently the [[color commentator]] on [[WMVP]] for Chicago Bears broadcasts.

'''Tom Wittum''' (January 11, 1950 – January 22, 2010) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player. He had a 5-year career in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1973 to 1977 as a [[Punter (football position)|punter]]. He played in two [[Pro Bowls]] as a member of the [[San Francisco 49ers]].

A native of Berwyn, Ill., Wittum grew up in nearby Round Lake. A fifth-round pick of the Chicago White Sox in 1968, Wittum opted to attend [[Northern Illinois University]] instead.<ref name="twobittheap">[http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/n/a/2010/01/26/sports/s185819S19.DTL "Ex-San Francisco Pro Bowl punter Tom Wittum dies," ''The Associated Press'', Wednesday, January 27, 2010.]{{dead link|date=February 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> He was a three-year letter-winner in football for the Huskies from 1969 to 1971, and lettered four years (1969–72) as a third baseman for the NIU baseball team. He was inducted into the NIU Hall of Fame in 1987 and was a member of the Huskies' 1972 NCAA baseball team enshrined in 2008.

Wittum graduated from Northern Illinois with 10 kicking records, including the school's career, single-season and single-game records for punts, punting yards and punting average.<ref name="twobittheap"/> For his career, he averaged 40.39 yards on 228 punts for 9,210 total yards, numbers which as of January 2010 rank third, fourth and third, respectively, in the Huskie record book. As of January 2010 he still holds the top three single season totals for punts and punting yards with 78 for 3,129.

Wittum ranks eighth all-time at NIU in points by a kicker with 113 on 21 field goals and 50 PATs, all NIU records at the time. His career field-goal totals of 21 made on 37 attempts, also school records at the time, are the eighth and seventh-most in school history. He made 50 of 55 extra-point attempts from 1969 to 1971 and is eighth in the Huskie record book in those categories.

Wittum shares the Pro Bowl record for longest punt with [[Darren Bennett (football player)|Darren Bennett]] (64 yards).  He also currently holds the No. 2 spot for most punts in a Pro Bowl game (9).

In 1978, Wittum retired from the NFL after a serious car accident left him with several broken bones.  After retirement as a player, he was head coach of the [[Grayslake, Illinois|Grayslake Central High School team in Illinois]] and  taught in addition driver's education. He died of cancer on January 22, 2010.<ref name="twobittheap"/>

Stowers Jr.''' (born November 18, 1966) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New Orleans Saints]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs]]. Stowers was selected by the [[San Diego Chargers]] in the eleventh round with the 283rd overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1990 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1990/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-25 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Holbreich |first=Curt |title=NFL ROUNDUP : Chargers, Archer Agree to Terms |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-07-19-sp-328-story.html |access-date=October 20, 2018 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=July 19, 1990}}</ref> He earned a degree in marketing.<ref name=trading>{{cite web |title=1992 Ultimate WLAF #125 Tommie Stowers - Orlando Thunder |url=https://www.tradingcarddb.com/CollectionGalleryP.cfm/pid/57363/Tommie-Stowers?Member=jeff%20davis&CollectionID=1&Filter=G |website=Trading Card Database |access-date=October 20, 2018}}</ref>

Stowers joined the [[Orlando Thunder]] of the [[World League of American Football]] (WLAF) in the 1991 season. He changed positions to tight end and rushed for 167 yards and one touchdown while receiving 156 yards.<ref name=trading/> The following year, he signed with the [[New Orleans Saints]] and played in 12 games, catching four passes for 23 yards. He played in four games with the Saints in 1993 but did not record any statistics. In 1994, Stowers joined the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and played in one game without catching and passes or rushing for any yards.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tommie Stowers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/StowTo20.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=October 20, 2018}}</ref> In 1996, he signed with the [[Orlando Predators]] of the [[Arena Football League]] but never played.<ref>{{cite news |title=Football |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1996/01/12/football-813/ |access-date=October 20, 2018 |work=[[Orlando Sentinel]] |date=January 12, 1996}}</ref> He played with the [[Rhein Fire (NFL Europe)|Rhein Fire]] of the WLAF in 1996.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tommie Stowers |url=https://www.footballdb.com/players/tommie-stowers-stoweto01 |website=The Football Database |access-date=October 20, 2018}}</ref>
